category_feedback.specific_evidence: expanded_walkthrough.title = 'When the child confuses $5 and $10 by colour' with recovery_moves = ['Use chart.', 'Compare faces.', 'Drill colour names.'] — this names a perceptual colour-discrimination issue, not a research-grounded G1 money misconception, and the recovery moves are one-to-three-word generic prompts a substitute could not actually follow.
category_feedback.required_fix: Replace the trap with a real G1 F1.1 misconception: child treats bill VALUE by front-digit or physical size (says $5 > $20 because '5 > 2'). Recovery should branch: digit-based — read the WHOLE numeral aloud ('twenty, not two'); size-based — lay bills end-to-end and say 'size does not tell value, the NUMBER does'. Anchor in value-vs-magnitude research.

category_feedback.specific_evidence: Lesson teaches identification almost entirely by COLOUR (blue=$5, purple=$10, green=$20) and 'Cassie says — colour first, value second!' Conceptual VALUE work is one throwaway line ('1 toonie + 1 fiver = $7') with no scaffolding, comparison, or composition. Money is treated as a colour-recognition task rather than a quantity/value concept.
category_feedback.required_fix: Re-anchor the lesson on VALUE as the math object, with colour as a secondary cue. Define 'value' precisely. Add a composition move where children build the same dollar amount two ways (e.g., $10 = one $10 OR two $5s). Have pairs invent a way to make $15 or $20 with the bills, then compare strategies — meeting the L3 'manipulatives carry meaning' bar.

summary: Lesson 3 is well-organized, child-friendly, and uses Cassie consistently, but it treats money as a colour-matching task rather than a value/quantity concept. The named trap is colour discrimination, not a real G1 money misconception, and recovery moves are vague. Worksheet does not need changes — fix the lesson's trap and re-anchor on VALUE so the existing parts read as transfer of taught content.
